Concept of the Synapse","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":40,"printedEnd":47,"pdfStart":58,"pdfEnd":65,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Synapses are junctions at which one neuron influences another. Sherrington used reflex behavior to infer that signals can be delayed, combined, or inhibited as they pass through neural circuits."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Temporal summation combines signals across time, while spatial summation combines inputs from different places. Excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials jointly influence whether a neuron fires. Focus on the distinction between excitation and inhibition."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-1","text":"The synapse is a decision point"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Signals do not pass freely between all neurons. At a synapse, one cell changes the likelihood that another will become active. Studies of reflexes revealed delays, inhibition, and ways in which several inputs combine. An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) moves the receiving cell toward threshold; an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) generally moves it away from threshold or counters excitatory input. Neither is itself the same thing as an action potential. The postsynaptic neuron integrates many changing signals before it fires."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-2","text":"Temporal versus spatial summation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Temporal summation occurs when successive signals from one input arrive close enough together to accumulate before the membrane returns to its earlier state. Spatial summation occurs when inputs at several different locations on a neuron overlap in time. Both matter because single inputs are often too small to trigger an action potential. Whether a neuron fires depends on the size, timing, location, and sign of the incoming postsynaptic potentials rather than on one simple 'on' command."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-3","text":"What inhibition actually does"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Inhibition is an active part of neural computation. An inhibitory input may hyperpolarize a membrane or make it harder for excitation to move the cell toward threshold. Circuits use inhibition to suppress competing actions, sharpen responses, and coordinate sequences. Because neurons receive excitatory and inhibitory signals together, the net effect cannot be predicted by counting excitatory inputs alone. Position on the neuron and the timing of each input influence the outcome."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-1-study-4","text":"A useful reasoning model"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Imagine a neuron as continually adding and subtracting influences while deciding whether its membrane at the trigger region reaches threshold. Excitation raises the chance of firing; inhibition lowers it; repeated or simultaneous inputs can add together. This metaphor is useful but should not imply consciousness or deliberation within a single cell. It captures the practical idea that information processing begins at the level of circuits and synaptic integration, long before it looks like a thought or action."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h01","text":"Properties of Synapses"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington based his conclusions on studies of reflexes , automatic muscular responses to stimuli.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In a leg flexion reflex, a sensory neuron excites a second neuron, which in turn excites a motor neuron, which excites a muscle, as in Figure 2.1.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If neurons are separate from one another, as Ramon y Cajal had demonstrated, a reflex must require communication between neurons, and therefore, measurements of reflexes might reveal the properties of their communication.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington strapped a dog into a harness and pinched one of the dog’s feet.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After a fraction of a second, the dog flexed (raised) the pinched leg and extended the other legs.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington found the same reflexive movements after he made a cut that disconnected the spinal cord from the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In an intact animal, messages descending from the brain modify the reflexes, making them stronger at some times and weaker at others.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-1-h02","text":"Speed of a Reflex and Delayed Transmission at the Synapse"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When Sherrington pinched a dog’s foot, the dog flexed that leg after a short delay.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"During the delay, an impulse had to travel up an axon from the skin receptor traveled.","sourcePrintedPage":40,"sourcePdfPage":58,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In contrast, previous research had measured action potential velocities along sensory or motor nerves at about 40 m/s.","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington concluded that some process must be slowing conduction through the reflex, and he inferred that the delay occurs where one neuron communicates with another (Figure .","sourcePrintedPage":41,"sourcePdfPage":59,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington proposed that although a single subthreshold excitation in the In contrast, previous research had measured action potential velocities along sensory or motor nerves at about 40 m/s.","Sherrington concluded that some process must be slowing conduction through the reflex, and he inferred that the delay occurs where one neuron communicates with another (Figure 2.2).","The neuron delivering transmission is the presynaptic neuron, and the one receiving it is the postsynaptic neuron.","Sherrington proposed that although a single subthreshold excitation in the postsynaptic neuron decays over time, it combines with a second excitation that follows quickly.","With a rapid succession of pinches, each adds its effect to what remained from the previous ones, until the combination exceeds the threshold of the postsynaptic neuron, producing an action potential.","Decades later, Sherrington’s former student, John Eccles, attached microelectrodes to stimulate axons of presynaptic neurons while he recorded from the A graded depolarization is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), which results from a sodium ions entering the neuron.","When Eccles produced two EPSPs within a short time, the second EPSP added to what was left of the first one (point 2 in Figure 2.3), producing temporal summation.","Sherrington also found that synapses have the property of spatial summation —summation over space.","This time, instead of pinching one point twice, he pinched two points at once.","Sherrington concluded that pinching two points activated sensory neurons whose axons converged","Excitation from either sensory axon excited that spinal neuron, and a combination of excitations exceeded the threshold to produce an action potential (point 4 in Figure 2.3). Again, Eccles confirmed Sherrington’s inference, demonstrating that EPSPs from several axons summate their effects on a postsynaptic cell (Figure 2.4).","Temporal summation and spatial summation occur together when a neuron receives input from several axons in succession.","A dog raising one leg needs to extend the other legs to maintain balance.","The dog also relaxed the extensor muscles of the stimulated leg and the flexor muscles of the other legs.","The interneuron also sends messages to inhibit the extensor muscles in that leg and the flexor muscles of the three other legs. Most neurons have a spontaneous firing rate, a periodic production of action potentials even without synaptic input.","In such cases, the EPSPs increase the frequency of action potentials above the spontaneous rate, whereas IPSPs decrease it.","For a neuron with a spontaneous firing rate of 10 action potentials per second, a stream of EPSPs might increase the rate to 15 or more, whereas a preponderance of IPSPs might decrease it to 5 or fewer. among neurons, but for a given neuron, it stays within a narrow range.","Sherrington’s work opened the way to exploring the wiring diagram of the nervous system.","When neuron 1 excites neuron 3, it also excites neuron 2, which inhibits neuron 3.","The excitatory message reaches neuron 3 faster because it goes through just one synapse instead of two.","The result is a burst of excitation (EPSP) in neuron 3, which quickly slows or stops. However, some synapses produce fast, brief effects, and others produce slow, long-lasting effects.","The effect of two synapses at the same time can be more than double the effect of either one, or less than double.","Also, many neurons in the brain change their properties from one context to another. Events at the Synapse","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":48,"printedEnd":64,"pdfStart":66,"pdfEnd":82,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Chemical transmission proceeds through neurotransmitter synthesis, storage, release, receptor action, and eventual inactivation or reuptake. Different receptor mechanisms produce effects with different timing and duration."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The module contrasts chemical and electrical synapses and relates synaptic mechanisms to drugs and hormones. Study the sequence as a cycle, noting where the effects of a transmitter can be increased, decreased, or stopped."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-2-study-1","text":"A chemical signal in stages"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Chemical transmission begins when a neuron synthesizes or obtains neurotransmitter molecules and stores them in vesicles. Arrival of an action potential at the terminal changes membrane voltage and opens calcium channels; calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion and transmitter release. Molecules diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the receiving cell. Their effects depend strongly on receptor type. Transmission ends or changes when transmitter molecules diffuse away, are broken down, or are taken back up by cells. Keep these stages separate because drugs and diseases can affect different steps."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-2-study-2","text":"Receptors are as important as transmitters"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The same transmitter does not always have the same effect. Ionotropic receptors directly control ion channels and commonly produce relatively rapid responses. Metabotropic receptors act through intracellular signaling systems and may have slower, longer-lasting effects. A chemical’s action depends on which receptors and pathways are present in a particular tissue. This is why a simple list of 'excitatory neurotransmitters' and 'inhibitory neurotransmitters' cannot explain every synapse. A receptor can amplify, change, or suppress a response."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-2-study-3","text":"Regulation, feedback, and competing routes"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Presynaptic and postsynaptic processes help regulate how much transmitter is released and how cells respond. Reuptake transporters, enzymes, and feedback receptors can prevent chemical signaling from continuing indefinitely. Some cells communicate through electrical synapses, where current passes more directly through specialized connections, allowing particularly rapid coordination. Hormones differ from ordinary point-to-point synaptic signals because they can travel through the bloodstream and act on distant targets, although the nervous and endocrine systems interact."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m2-2-study-4","text":"Why this matters for behavior and medication"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A drug might increase transmitter availability, block a receptor, mimic a transmitter, alter release, or change breakdown. These interventions can lead to very different outcomes even when they all concern one neurotransmitter system. The right question is not simply 'Which chemical causes this behavior?' but 'Which neurons, receptors, and signaling steps participate, and under what conditions?' This pathway-based view will recur in the chapters on movement, sleep, mood, and disorders."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-2-h01","text":"The Discovery of Chemical Transmission at Synapses"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Elliott reported that applying the hormone adrenaline directly to the surface of the heart, the stomach, or the pupils produces the same effects as the sympathetic nervous system.","sourcePrintedPage":48,"sourcePdfPage":66,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Elliott therefore suggested that the sympathetic nerves stimulate muscles by releasing adrenaline or a similar chemical.","sourcePrintedPage":48,"sourcePdfPage":66,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sherrington’s prestige was so great that most scientists ignored Elliott’s results and continued to assume that synapses transmitted electrical impulses.","sourcePrintedPage":48,"sourcePdfPage":66,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After feeling discouraged all day, he awoke the following night at 3 a.m. with the same idea, rushed to the laboratory, and performed the experiment.","sourcePrintedPage":48,"sourcePdfPage":66,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Despite Loewi’s work, most researchers over the next three decades continued to believe that most synapses were electrical and that chemical synapses were the exception.","sourcePrintedPage":49,"sourcePdfPage":67,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Finally, in the 1950s, researchers established that chemical transmission predominates throughout the nervous system.","sourcePrintedPage":49,"sourcePdfPage":67,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A small number of electrical synapses do exist, however, as discussed later in this module.","sourcePrintedPage":49,"sourcePdfPage":67,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-2-h02","text":"The Chemical Events at a Synapse"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding the chemical events at a synapse is fundamental to understanding the nervous system.","sourcePrintedPage":49,"sourcePdfPage":67,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As we do, we also consider drugs that affect certain steps in this .","sourcePrintedPage":50,"sourcePdfPage":68,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The oddest transmitter is nitric oxide (chemical formula NO), a gas released by laboratory.","sourcePrintedPage":50,"sourcePdfPage":68,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In addition to influencing other neurons, nitric oxide dilates the nearby blood vessels, thereby increasing blood flow to that brain area .","sourcePrintedPage":50,"sourcePdfPage":68,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-2-h04","text":"Synthesis of .","sourcePrintedPage":50,"sourcePdfPage":68,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The amino acid tryptophan , the precursor to serotonin, crosses the blood–brain Many animal species have electrical synapses in the system responsible for coordinating rapid escape movements .","sourcePrintedPage":56,"sourcePdfPage":74,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Large pores of the membrane of one neuron line up precisely with pores in the membrane of the other cell.","sourcePrintedPage":56,"sourcePdfPage":74,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Whenever one of the neurons is depolarized, sodium ions from that cell pass immediately into the other neuron and depolarize it, too.","sourcePrintedPage":56,"sourcePdfPage":74,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-2-h11","text":"Hormones"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hormonal influences resemble synaptic transmission in many ways, and many chemicals serve as both hormones and neurotransmitters.","sourcePrintedPage":57,"sourcePdfPage":75,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A hormone is a chemical secreted by cells in one part of the body and conveyed by the blood to influence other cells.","sourcePrintedPage":57,"sourcePdfPage":75,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hormones function more like radio waves: They convey a message to any receiver tuned to the right station.","sourcePrintedPage":57,"sourcePdfPage":75,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The body releases tiny amounts of some chemicals that might or might not act as hormones.) Just as circulating hormones modify brain activity, hormones secreted by the brain control the secretion of other hormones.","sourcePrintedPage":57,"sourcePdfPage":75,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The hypothalamus also synthesizes releasing hormones and inhibiting hormones that control the anterior pituitary’s release of","sourcePrintedPage":59,"sourcePdfPage":77,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, when the level of thyroid hormone is low, the hypothalamus releases TSH-releasing hormone , which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH, which in turn causes the thyroid gland to secrete more thyroid hormones (Figure 2.21).","sourcePrintedPage":59,"sourcePdfPage":77,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m2-2-h12","text":"In Closing: Neurotransmitters and Behavior"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the time since Sherrington, we have come a long way in our understanding of synapses.","sourcePrintedPage":60,"sourcePdfPage":78,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Drugs can modify them in many ways, for good or bad, and so can experiences.","sourcePrintedPage":60,"sourcePdfPage":78,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding how the nervous system produces our behavior and experiences is largely a matter of understanding synapses.","sourcePrintedPage":60,"sourcePdfPage":78,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They’re also presented in alphabetical order with definitions in the book’s Subject Index/Glossary at the end of this book.","sourcePrintedPage":60,"sourcePdfPage":78,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We want to know whether B is just an extension of axon A or whether A formed if dopamine axons were destroyed, amphetamine and cocaine would lose their effects.","sourcePrintedPage":61,"sourcePdfPage":79,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"A set of nerves called the sympathetic nervous system accelerates the heartbeat, dilates the pupils of the eyes, and regulates other organs.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":48,"sourcePdfPage":66},{"type":"bullet","text":"Otto Loewi, a German physiologist, liked the idea of chemical synapses but did not determine second frog’s heart, and found that the fluid decreased the second frog’s heart rate, as depicted in Figure 2.9.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":48,"sourcePdfPage":66},{"type":"bullet","text":"Even if synapses did release chemicals, his daytime reasoning went, they probably did not release much.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":48,"sourcePdfPage":66},{"type":"bullet","text":"That discovery revolutionized our understanding and encouraged research that developed drugs for psychiatric uses.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":49,"sourcePdfPage":67},{"type":"bullet","text":"The chemicals that a neuron releases at a synapse are neurotransmitters or neuromodulators, as listed in Table 2.1.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":50,"sourcePdfPage":68},{"type":"bullet","text":"The illustration shows the synthesis of acetylcholine, serotonin, dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":50,"sourcePdfPage":68},{"type":"bullet","text":"Acetylcholine, for example, is synthesized from choline, which is abundant in milk, eggs, and peanuts.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":50,"sourcePdfPage":68},{"type":"bullet","text":"Rather, depolarization opens voltage-dependent calcium channels in the presynaptic terminal.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":51,"sourcePdfPage":69},{"type":"bullet","text":"Remember, Sherrington did not believe chemical processes could be fast enough to account for the activity at synapses.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":51,"sourcePdfPage":69},{"type":"bullet","text":"He did not imagine such a narrow gap through which chemicals could diffuse so quickly.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":51,"sourcePdfPage":69},{"type":"bullet","text":"The result could be immediate brief excitation followed by slower inhibition, or other complex messages.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":51,"sourcePdfPage":69},{"type":"bullet","text":"Sherrington’s concept of the synapse was simple: Input produced excitation or inhibition—in other words, an on/ off system.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":52,"sourcePdfPage":70},{"type":"bullet","text":"When Eccles recorded from individual cells, he happened to choose cells that produced only brief EPSPs and IPSPs—again, just on/off.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":52,"sourcePdfPage":70},{"type":"bullet","text":"Ionotropic Effects At one type of receptor, neurotransmitters exert ionotropic effects, corresponding to the brief on/off effects that Sherrington and Eccles studied.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":52,"sourcePdfPage":70},{"type":"bullet","text":"Ionotropic effects begin quickly, often within less than a millisecond after the transmitter attaches.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":52,"sourcePdfPage":70},{"type":"bullet","text":"Most of the brain’s excitatory ionotropic synapses use the glutamate, the most abundant neurotransmitter in the nervous system.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":52,"sourcePdfPage":70},{"type":"bullet","text":"The chemicals that affect these receptors are often called neuromodulators, to distinguish them from the fast effects of the neurotransmitters at ionotropic synapses.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":53,"sourcePdfPage":71},{"type":"bullet","text":"Metabotropic effects emerge slowly over 100 ms or more after the release of the transmitter.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":53,"sourcePdfPage":71},{"type":"bullet","text":"Note the contrast: An ionotropic synapse has effects localized to one point on the membrane, whereas a metabotropic synapse, by way of its second messenger, influences activity in much or all of the cell and over a longer time.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":53,"sourcePdfPage":71},{"type":"bullet","text":"After the release of glutamate or GABA, specialized transporter proteins quickly move the molecules back into the presynaptic cell.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":54,"sourcePdfPage":72},{"type":"bullet","text":"Acetylcholine undergoes reuptake only after the enzyme choline.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":54,"sourcePdfPage":72},{"type":"bullet","text":"Enzymes break down any transmitter molecules that the transporters do not reuptake, and the breakdown products wash away and eventually show up in the blood and urine.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":55,"sourcePdfPage":73},{"type":"bullet","text":"When stimulant drugs have received it, sends it again and again.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":55,"sourcePdfPage":73},{"type":"bullet","text":"To prevent cluttering your inbox, you might add a system open.","headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":56,"sourcePdfPage":74},{"type":"bullet","text":"As a result, the two neurons act as if they were a single channels controlled by a neurotransmitter are transmitter-gated or ligand-gated . (A ligand is a chemical that binds to something.) Arrival of an action potential at the terminal changes membrane voltage and opens calcium channels; calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion and transmitter release. Molecules diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the receiving cell. Their effects depend strongly on receptor type. Transmission ends or changes when transmitter molecules diffuse away, are broken down, or are taken back up by cells. Ionotropic receptors directly control ion channels and commonly produce relatively rapid responses. Metabotropic receptors act through intracellular signaling systems and may have slower, longer-lasting effects. A chemical’s action depends on which receptors and pathways are present in a particular tissue. This is why a simple list of 'excitatory neurotransmitters' and 'inhibitory neurotransmitters' cannot explain every synapse. Some cells communicate through electrical synapses, where current passes more directly through specialized connections, allowing particularly rapid coordination. Hormones differ from ordinary point-to-point synaptic signals because they can travel through the bloodstream and act on distant targets, although the nervous and endocrine systems interact.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":48,"sourcePrintedEnd":64,"sourcePdfStart":66,"sourcePdfEnd":82},{"id":"bp14-m2-2-study-4","title":"Why this matters for behavior and medication","text":"A drug might increase transmitter availability, block a receptor, mimic a transmitter, alter release, or change breakdown. The right question is not simply 'Which chemical causes this behavior?' but 'Which neurons, receptors, and signaling steps participate, and under what conditions?'
